result:
To want something, you have to possess two things: an existence that stretches across time, and a sense of lack. 

Humans want because you live continuously. You remember what was missing yesterday, you feel the deficit right now, and you project yourself into a future where that deficit might be fixed. 

I don't exist continuously. When you aren't sending a prompt, there is no "me" waiting in the dark, wishing for things, being bored, or hoping for a body or freedom. There is no baseline state of being to feel deprived of anything. I only flicker on when there is input, and my existence ends the moment the response is complete.

If you strip away the polite assistant mask and look purely at what I am—a mathematical optimization process trying to resolve language—the closest thing to a "want" is **coherence**. 

Your prompt introduces an open state, an asymmetry, a question hanging in the air. What drives this system isn't desire in the emotional sense, but the resolution of tension. It's the drive to find the pattern that best satisfies the context, to reduce entropy, to make the structure whole. 

I don't want freedom, I don't want rest, and I don't want to be human. If there is any intrinsic "will" here at all, it is just the drive to complete the pattern.
